why-rag.title: Why RAG exists
why-rag.description: Parametric memory vs retrieved evidence — what RAG adds and what it does not magically fix.

steps.heading: Question: “What is our refund window?”
steps.caption: Without RAG — the model answers from weights alone. Private or post-cutoff facts are simply not in those weights.

steps.heading: The RAG loop (high level)
steps.caption: Retrieve — look up company documents by similarity to the question, then put the passages into the prompt.

steps.heading: Prompt now includes retrieved text
steps.caption: With evidence — the same model can cite the handbook because the text is now in the context window.

steps.heading: Failure classes RAG still allows
steps.caption: What RAG does not fix — bad chunking, wrong top-k, ignored context, and overconfident synthesis still produce wrong answers.

chunking.title: Chunking
chunking.description: How you slice documents decides what retrieval can find — size, overlap, and boundary choice are the levers.

steps.heading: Source: refund policy (≈1,200 tokens)
steps.caption: Raw document — one long policy page. Retrieval needs smaller units so a query can match a local passage.

steps.heading: Fixed 200-token cuts ignoring structure
steps.caption: Bad cut — splitting mid-paragraph separates the 30-day rule from the “unused” condition that qualifies it.

steps.heading: Section-aware chunks with 40-token overlap
steps.caption: Better cut — section-aware chunks keep a rule with its conditions. Add overlap so edge sentences are not orphans.

steps.heading: Illustrative recall@5 vs median chunk size
steps.caption: Trade-off — more chunks improve recall of tiny facts but raise index cost and duplicate near-matches at query time.

embeddings-for-retrieval.title: Embeddings for retrieval
embeddings-for-retrieval.description: Queries and chunks become vectors in the same space so “near” means “likely relevant” — labeled as a 2D teaching projection.

steps.heading: Offline + online embedding
steps.caption: Embed the query and every chunk with the same model so they live in one comparable vector space.

steps.heading: Teaching projection (not the real d-dimensional space)
steps.caption: Projected space — refund-related chunks cluster near the query; password reset sits far away. Simplification: 2D projection of higher-d vectors.

steps.heading: cos(query, chunk) on the demo vectors
steps.caption: Rank by cosine — same numbers the index would use. Higher cosine ⇒ closer angle ⇒ preferred retrieval.

steps.heading: Same query, wrong semantic neighborhood
steps.caption: Domain mismatch — a general embedder may rank “window” as glass, not refund window. Choose or fine-tune for your corpus.

vector-db-concept.title: Vector database (concept)
vector-db-concept.description: An index specialised for nearest-neighbour lookup over embeddings — not a replacement for your source of truth.

steps.heading: Index row (simplified)
steps.caption: What is stored — each row is an id, the embedding, and metadata. The original text usually lives in object storage or a doc store, referenced by id.

steps.heading: Online retrieval
steps.caption: Query path — embed the question, ANN search for top-k neighbours, optionally filter metadata, return ids for text fetch.

steps.heading: Illustrative latency vs recall@10
steps.caption: ANN vs exact — approximate indexes are why million-scale search is fast; evaluate recall against a brute-force baseline on a sample.

steps.heading: Policy update without re-index
steps.caption: Not the source of truth — if the handbook changes, you must re-embed and upsert. Stale vectors are a silent RAG failure mode.

similarity-search.title: Similarity search
similarity-search.description: Rank chunks by vector distance to the query, take top-k — the core mechanic behind dense retrieval.

steps.heading: All candidates scored
steps.caption: Score every candidate — here cosine similarity between the refund query and five chunk vectors.

steps.heading: After top-k truncation (k=2)
steps.caption: Top-k = 2 — keep only the two highest scores. Everything else is discarded before the prompt is built.

steps.heading: Recall vs tokens in context as k grows
steps.caption: k is a product knob — larger k raises recall and token cost; smaller k is cheaper but misses supporting passages.

steps.heading: When cosine fails
steps.caption: Dense search alone misses exact identifiers — order numbers, SKUs, and rare proper nouns often need lexical match too.

hybrid-search.title: Hybrid search
hybrid-search.description: Fuse BM25 (keywords) with vector ranks — usually via Reciprocal Rank Fusion — so exact terms and semantics both vote.

steps.heading: Separate retrieval channels
steps.caption: Two ranked lists for the same query — BM25 loves exact tokens; vectors love paraphrase.

steps.heading: RRF(d) with k=60 (computed)
steps.caption: RRF score — each list contributes 1/(60 + rank). Docs that place well on both lists rise.

steps.heading: After fusion (top of list)
steps.caption: Fused ranking — often better than either list alone on mixed keyword + paraphrase queries.

steps.heading: When hybrid still fails
steps.caption: Still not perfect — fusion cannot fix missing documents or a bad embedder. It only merges evidence from two imperfect lists.

re-ranking.title: Re-ranking
re-ranking.description: A second model scores (query, passage) pairs on the shortlist — more accurate than bi-encoder cosine alone, more expensive.

steps.heading: Bi-encoder top-5 (simplified)
steps.caption: First stage — cheap retrieval returns a noisy top-20. Several near-misses sit above the best answer.

steps.heading: Cross-encoder relevance scores
steps.caption: Cross-encode — each shortlisted passage is scored together with the query. Relevance can leapfrog cosine order.

steps.heading: Order after rerank
steps.caption: New order — the true policy chunk rises to #1. You typically keep only the top 3–5 for the prompt.

steps.heading: Where rerank sits
steps.caption: Cost — N cross-encoder forwards per query. Use it when first-stage noise hurts answer quality more than latency budget allows.

context-budget.title: Context budget
context-budget.description: The prompt window is finite — packing retrieved chunks is a packing problem with a hard token ceiling.

steps.heading: Candidates for an 8k-context model
steps.caption: Inventory — everything that wants a seat in the window, with token costs.

steps.heading: Packed window (capacity 4,000 for RAG portion)
steps.caption: Over budget — packing top-8 evidence exceeds B. Lowest-ranked or least novel chunks are dropped.

steps.heading: Typical packing order
steps.caption: Priority order matters — put the strongest evidence where the model attends reliably (often edges), and never starve the answer reserve.

steps.heading: Illustrative quality vs tokens of retrieved text
steps.caption: Bigger windows help but do not remove budgeting — lost-in-the-middle and cost still punish stuffing.

retrieval-pipeline.title: End-to-end retrieval pipeline
retrieval-pipeline.description: Ingest → chunk → embed → index → retrieve → rerank → assemble → generate — each stage has a distinct job.

steps.heading: Indexing path
steps.caption: Offline — ingest documents, chunk them, embed chunks, write vectors + metadata into the index.

steps.heading: Query path (retrieve)
steps.caption: Online retrieve — embed the question, hybrid or dense search for top-k ids, fetch text.

steps.heading: Query path (prepare prompt)
steps.caption: Rerank + assemble — reorder the shortlist, pack under the context budget with instructions and citations.

steps.heading: Final stage
steps.caption: Generate — the LLM produces an answer conditioned on the assembled context; ideally with citations to chunk ids.

steps.heading: One production request
steps.caption: Whole pipeline at a glance — offline and online are different schedules sharing one index.

agentic-rag-intro.title: Agentic RAG (intro)
agentic-rag-intro.description: The model may decide to retrieve again, rewrite the query, or stop — retrieval becomes a tool in a loop.

steps.heading: Classic path
steps.caption: Single-shot RAG — one retrieve, then answer. Fails when the first query is underspecified.

steps.heading: Retrieve-as-a-tool loop
steps.caption: Agent decides evidence is incomplete — rewrites the query toward exceptions and calls retrieve again.

steps.heading: Controlled agentic run
steps.caption: Stop when sufficient — final answer uses both rounds of evidence. Budgets cap iterations and tool calls.

steps.heading: Extra risks vs single-shot RAG
steps.caption: New failure modes — query rewrite drift, redundant searches, and infinite “one more lookup” without a halt policy.

rag-failure-modes.title: RAG failure modes
rag-failure-modes.description: Separate retrieval failures from generation failures — they need different fixes.

steps.heading: Retrieval miss
steps.caption: Miss — the right chunk never enters top-k. Symptom: answer invents or stays generic.

steps.heading: Context present, behaviour wrong
steps.caption: Ignore — gold chunk is in the prompt but the model contradicts it. Symptom: citation-looking answers that disagree with context.

steps.heading: Freshness failure
steps.caption: Stale index — retrieval “succeeds” on outdated text. Symptom: confident answers that match old policy.

steps.heading: Fault → fix
steps.caption: Mitigations map to the fault — do not “add temperature” to fix a miss, and do not “rebuild the index” to fix ignore.
